headline: Vance Says H-1B Attack Targeted Companies, Not Visa Holders Themselves
subheadline: At a CBS News town hall in Michigan, the vice president said his rhetoric had been imperfect, invoked his South Indian in-laws, and said his criticism was of employers and the visa system — not H-1B holders.
body:
• At a CBS News town hall on Saturday, Vance said his "foreign indentured servants" description was not a criticism of visa holders, but of companies and a visa system that ties a worker's stay to one employer.
  • Vance conceded his wording was flawed — "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me" — and invoked his family: "I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India."
  • He did not withdraw the underlying policy: he still argues some large employers lay off American workers while hiring H-1B staff who cannot easily push back on pay or conditions.
  • For H-1B holders and employers: no rule changed in this interview — your status and PERM position are unchanged — but employer hiring and layoff practices remain under scrutiny, so keep petitions, wage records and job-change paperwork current.

Vice President JD Vance has clarified his description of H-1B workers as "foreign indentured servants," saying the criticism was aimed at American companies and the visa system, not at the visa holders themselves. At a CBS News town hall in Flat Rock, Michigan, on Saturday, Vance acknowledged his rhetoric had been imperfect after a voter who had immigrated to the United States challenged him for scapegoating immigrants.

"You know where my family comes from, and I love my mother-in-law and father-in-law who immigrated from South India, and obviously their daughter, born in the United States of America, is now the second lady, and I'm very proud of her, and I love her very much." — Vice President JD Vance, CBS News town hall

What Vance Said

Vance said his point was about leverage. A company certifies it cannot find an American applicant, brings in an H-1B worker, and that worker's visa becomes, in his words, their only lifeline to the United States. A worker who complains risks losing the job and, with it, the right to stay. "That's not a criticism of the H-1B visa holder. That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker," he said, according to Livemint's account of the town hall.

He put it as a criticism of the system itself. "It's a criticism of the visa system that allows people to be treated effectively as indentured servants that can be shipped back to their country of origin," Vance said, as reported by YourStory. Pressed on whether the administration's rhetoric dehumanised immigrants, he replied: "My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant. And in fact, I love a number of immigrants."

He gave a concrete example: a trillion-dollar company that brings in an accountant from abroad, says it cannot hire from its existing labour pool, and fires an accountant already on the payroll. That, he said, was not fairness. He called for a balance — welcome for people who contribute, paired with scrutiny of corporations that replace existing staff.

How We Got Here

The row began earlier this month, when Vance announced the suspension of several firms, including Indian IT companies, from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme, known as PERM — the first step towards an employment-based green card. Companies named in coverage included Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. Announcing the move, Vance urged companies to stop importing an indentured servant to do a job an American worker would happily do.

India protested formally. The Ministry of External Affairs said the description was unwarranted and deeply offensive, carried painful historical and colonial connotations, and ignored the fact that Indian professionals are highly educated, skilled contributors to the US economy. Indian professionals account for over 70% of all approved H-1B petitions annually. Saturday's town hall is the first time Vance has personally conceded fault in his own wording.

What It Means

For H-1B holders, the distinction matters politically, though it changes no regulation. Vance is now on record separating the worker from the employer: the worker, in his account, is exposed to pressure because status depends on the sponsoring job. That framing does not restore any suspended firm's PERM access or alter petition rules. Holders considering a job change should still treat timing, portability filings and documentation as critical.

For employers, the message is harder. Vance defended the diagnosis while apologising for the delivery. Companies that lay off American staff while sponsoring H-1B workers in similar roles are the stated target of administration scrutiny. Sponsors should expect hiring records, wage levels and layoff history to be the evidence that counts.

Vance announced no new policy and did not retract his support for tighter controls. What changed is who he says the criticism belongs to — and an acknowledgement that the way he said it was on him.
